title: Fixed rain-gauge networks confirmed post-1997 runoff deficits in south-east Australia and the eastern US; both lost about 40 mm of runoff per year after 2009 (CAMELS, 1951-2025)
abstract:
Question: earlier work found that runoff in south-east Australia and in the eastern US fell below each catchment's 1951-1996 rainfall-runoff relation in 1997-1999 and stayed low. In Australia, the size of the shift with SILO rainfall was half of the size with AGCD rainfall. Do changes in the rain-gauge networks behind gridded rainfall cause these shifts? Why does the Australian shift look larger?

Approach: we made catchment rainfall indices from fixed networks of long-record GHCN-Daily gauges (732 Australian and 1,455 US candidates). A gauge stayed in a network only if it had complete data in 80% or more of the years of each era 1951-1996, 1997-2009 and 2010-end. We fitted sqrt(runoff) on rainfall, previous-year rainfall and temperature for 1951-1996, with each rainfall source on the same catchment-years (CAMELS-AUS v2.03 to 2021; CAMELS-US with USGS flow to water year 2025). We also split daily flow into baseflow and quickflow and expressed the deficits in SD units, mm per year and percent of runoff.

Results: with gauge rainfall, the mean residual was -0.77 SD (95% interval -1.05 to -0.51) in 1997-2009 and -0.78 SD (-1.03 to -0.51) in 2010-2021 in south-east Australia (114 catchments), and -0.42 and -0.47 SD (-0.62 to -0.26) in the eastern US (92). The western US stayed near zero. Coverage, temperature and calibration variants gave the same signs. SILO drifted 2.0% low relative to the gauges after 2009, which explains much of its smaller deficit. In 2010-end, runoff was 44 mm per year below the relation in south-east Australia and 42 mm per year in the eastern US (difference -2 mm, -22 to +17), about 4% of rainfall in both. As a fraction of runoff the deficit was 20% against 9%, because runoff ratios are lower in Australia (median 0.25 against 0.42). At runoff ratio 0.20-0.45, the regions did not clearly differ in any unit. Baseflow and quickflow both fell; baseflow carried 43% of the Australian volume deficit against a 38% baseflow index, and 41% against 42% in the eastern US.

Conclusion: the shifts are not gauge-network artifacts. A similar loss of water appears as a larger 'state shift' in low-runoff-ratio Australian catchments.

Limitations: the networks use the same gauges as the gridded products; small networks; one annual model form; cause not tested; the unit comparison is post hoc.

citations.reason: We reuse its US annual table and its 1951-1996 calibration test. Fixed-gauge rainfall confirms its south-east Australian and eastern US shifts; the unit comparison qualifies its 'similar size' statement.
The Victorian low-runoff state after the Millennium Drought is not an artifact of gauge network change.
Its larger deficit in dry Australian catchments agrees with an additive loss of similar mm size.
Its post-drought US null does not exclude a non-drought eastern US shift.
